title: Mobile crushers run without dust-suppression sprays, breaching PG3/16 permits, and councils act on neighbours' dust complaints
problem: Mobile crushing and screening plant (in demolition, recycling and quarries) is permitted under LAPPC guidance PG3/16. Typical permit conditions require water sprays at the feed and discharge points whenever the plant is crushing, and crushing must stop if the water supply fails. In practice operators crush with the hose off or the bowser empty. Councils investigate dust complaints, and offences carry fines of up to £50k in the magistrates' court. There is no record that the sprays ran.
who_suffers: Neighbours and site workers; the permit holder
buyer: Managing director or compliance manager of a mobile crushing, demolition or aggregate-recycling contractor (the permit holder)
industry: Mobile crushing and screening under LAPPC permits (PG3/16)
current_workaround: The operator's word that sprays were on, paper daily checklists, and a council officer visit after complaints
sensor_concept: Pressure switch or pulse flow sensor on the spray manifold, plus an accelerometer on the crusher chassis to tell crushing from idling. LTE-M, powered from the machine's 24 V. Logs minutes crushed without water, alerts the foreman, and exports a permit-compliance record for each site move.
notes: c4 strong: statutory permit conditions, council inspections, fines. c2: daily. c8 simple. c6 via crusher dealers and hire fleets (Finlay, Sandvik, Keestrack dealers) that already fit telematics. c7 looks unserved: OEM telematics track engine hours, not sprays.

title: Quarry silt lagoons overtop in storms and send sediment into rivers, while managers check freeboard by eye
problem: Sand-and-gravel and hard-rock quarries settle wash-plant water in lagoons. Heavy rain or a stuck pump causes overtopping or a breach, discolouring rivers for kilometres. EA and SEPA prosecutions follow: quarry fines of ~£3k–£12.5k plus costs, and a housebuilder was fined £100k for a lagoon overflow. Lagoons also count as 'tips' under the Quarries Regulations 1999, which require inspections and geotechnical appraisal.
who_suffers: Quarry managers; rivers and anglers downstream
buyer: Quarry manager or estates and environment manager at an independent quarry operator
industry: Quarry settlement lagoons and site water management
current_workaround: Visual freeboard checks during shift inspections, staff driving round the lagoons in storms, and gauge boards
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic level sensor on a post above each lagoon, a float switch at the overflow or spillway, and rainfall from an API. LoRaWAN or LTE-M with solar power. Alerts when freeboard falls below the limit, and keeps a continuous level record for the tips inspection file.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Tension cracks at quarry face and tip crests: daily shift inspections miss slow movement before a collapse
problem: The Quarries Regulations 1999 require geotechnical assessment of faces and tips, plus inspections before each shift and after heavy rain. Slow movement at a face crest or tip edge gives warning signs that the eye misses. A collapse can bury plant worth ~£ hundreds of thousands or kill someone, and HSE prosecutes. Wireless geotechnical monitoring exists but is priced for large mines and rail.
who_suffers: Quarry operatives working below faces and on tips; the quarry manager
buyer: Quarry manager of an independent quarry, advised by its geotechnical specialist
industry: Face and tip stability at UK quarries
current_workaround: Visual inspections, survey prisms read periodically by surveyors, and crack pins measured with a tape
sensor_concept: MEMS tilt node or draw-wire crack meter across the tension crack. LoRaWAN or LTE-M, 5-year battery. Alerts on rate-of-movement thresholds and writes a daily record to the excavations and tips register.
notes: filtered: safety-critical geotechnical monitoring

title: Quarry wheel wash broken or bypassed: mud on the public road brings council enforcement and crash claims
problem: Planning conditions require quarries to run wheel washes and keep public roads clean. When the pump fails, the sump fills with silt or drivers bypass the wash, mud and stone spread along the highway. Councils act on planning conditions or under the Highways Act, road sweepers are hired at ~£ hundreds a day, and claims follow from motorcyclists who crash.
who_suffers: Road users; the quarry operator facing complaints and claims
buyer: Quarry manager or operations manager of an aggregates or landfill-and-quarry operator
industry: Quarry and landfill site exits
current_workaround: Weighbridge staff watch the lorries, daily visual checks, and a sweeper on call
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the wash pump, an ultrasonic sensor for tank and silt level, and a magnetometer or radar vehicle counter at the wash bay and the bypass lane. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. A daily report shows vehicles washed against vehicles that bypassed, with alerts for pump faults and a full sump.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Seized conveyor pulley and idler bearings start belt fires at sand-and-gravel plants between daily belt walks
problem: A seized idler or tail-pulley bearing heats the belt until it burns or tears. A belt fire or rip stops production for days, with belt replacement costing ~£ thousands to tens of thousands plus lost output. Quarries walk their conveyors daily to meet PUWER and Quarries Regulations inspection duties, but still miss bearings that are heating up.
who_suffers: Plant fitters and operators; the quarry's production
buyer: Plant or engineering manager of an independent quarry or aggregates recycler
industry: Fixed conveyors at quarries and wash plants
current_workaround: Daily belt walks, listening, a handheld IR thermometer, and running bearings to failure
sensor_concept: Stick-on node with an accelerometer and temperature sensor on the head pulley, tail pulley and drive bearings. LoRaWAN, multi-year battery. Alerts on temperature or vibration trends, and keeps an inspection log that replaces part of the walk.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Fire suppression on quarry loaders and dumpers is discharged or depressurised, and nobody knows until the machine burns
problem: Insurers commonly expect fire suppression on high-value mobile plant such as loaders and haulers worth ~£250k+. Cylinders lose pressure, actuation lines get damaged, or systems are left disarmed after maintenance. An engine-bay fire writes off the machine and stops the quarry, and insurers can challenge the claim if the system wasn't maintained.
who_suffers: Machine operators; the plant manager; the insurer
buyer: Plant manager or insurance and risk manager of a quarry operator or plant hire firm
industry: Fire suppression on mobile plant in quarries and waste sites
current_workaround: Daily operator pre-use glance at the gauge, and a 6-monthly service by the suppression installer
sensor_concept: Pressure switch or transducer on the agent or actuation cylinder, plus engine-bay temperature. Standalone LTE-M unit on the machine's 24 V, with no CAN integration. Alerts on pressure loss or discharge, and sends the insurer a monthly 'armed' report.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Haul-road water bowsers sit idle on dry, windy days, breaching quarry dust-management planning conditions
problem: Mineral planning permissions require dust management schemes, which include damping haul roads in dry weather. The bowser sits idle when its driver is moved to another job. Dust reaches nearby houses, complaints pile up at liaison meetings, and councils or the EA take action or object to extensions. There is no record of when the roads were damped.
who_suffers: Neighbours; the quarry manager defending the operation
buyer: Quarry manager or environment manager of a quarry or landfill operator
industry: Haul-road dust suppression at quarries
current_workaround: Driver logbook, the manager's visual checks, and a complaints log
sensor_concept: GPS tracker and pulse flow sensor on the bowser spray bar, plus wind and humidity from a cheap on-site weather sensor. LTE-M. Maps which roads were damped against the weather, alerts when it is dry and windy and the bowser hasn't sprayed, and produces a monthly compliance report for liaison meetings.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Wash-plant flocculant dosing stops when the hopper or drum runs out, and dirty water reaches the lagoons and discharge point
problem: Wash plants and silt presses dose flocculant to settle fines. When the powder hopper or liquid drum runs out, or the dosing pump trips, the fines don't settle. The water circuit turns dirty, product goes out of spec, and silty water can reach the consented discharge. Lost production and re-washing cost ~£ thousands per shift, on top of the permit risk.
who_suffers: Wash-plant operators; the quarry's sales and environmental compliance
buyer: Plant manager at an aggregates or construction-and-demolition recycling wash plant
industry: Aggregate washing plants and water recycling
current_workaround: The operator checks the hopper level each shift; dosing-pump alarms sound only in the control cabin
sensor_concept: Load cell or tilt-level sensor on the flocculant hopper or drum, plus a current clamp on the dosing pump. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. Alerts on low stock and on the pump stopping, and logs consumption for the flocculant supplier, which can then auto-replenish.

title: Trespassers swim in flooded quarries every summer, and operators pay for security patrols and face drowning inquests
problem: In every hot spell, young people swim in cold, deep quarry lakes. Drownings are reported most summers and coroners criticise access control. Operators pay for security patrols (~£ hundreds per night) and fencing repairs, and carry Occupiers' Liability and reputational exposure.

buyer: Estates or security manager of a quarry operator with working or restored lakes
industry: Flooded working and restored quarries

title: Inflatable hirers leave bouncy castles with customers as the wind rises, and nobody measures the wind or notices the blower stop
problem: HSE guidance says no inflatable should be used in winds above 24 mph and that wind should be checked with an anemometer at regular intervals. At parties, fêtes and fairs, the operator often leaves the hirer in charge. A gust lifts the unit, or a tripped blower collapses it on children. In the Harlow case (2016), two operators were jailed for 3 years for gross negligence manslaughter after failing to monitor the wind. Insurance and PIPA inspection exist, but there is no proof that wind checks happened.
who_suffers: Children on the equipment; hire-company owners carrying criminal and civil liability

industry: Inflatable play equipment hire for parties, fêtes and events
current_workaround: A handheld anemometer if the operator is present, weather apps, and telling the hirer to 'deflate if windy'
sensor_concept: Low-cost cup anemometer on a short mast clipped to the unit, a current sensor or air-pressure switch on the blower, and an accelerometer on an anchor point. LTE-M. Sends SMS and voice-call alerts to the hirer and operator above 20 or 24 mph or when the blower stops, and keeps a hire log for the insurer and PIPA.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

problem: Since COVID, many venues hire marquees and stretch tents for months at a time. IStructE guidance on temporary demountable structures calls for a wind management plan with thresholds for inspection and evacuation, but out of hours nobody is watching. Storms rip covers, pull pegs and wreck frames (~£ thousands to £ tens of thousands per marquee), and a collapse onto guests brings HSE or council action.

buyer: Operations director of a marquee or stretch-tent hire company (MUTA member)
industry: Long-term marquee and temporary structure hire
current_workaround: Met Office warnings, phone calls from clients, and inspection visits after storms
sensor_concept: Mast-mounted anemometer plus accelerometer or tilt nodes on two frame legs or king poles to detect movement and uplift. LTE-M. Alerts the venue and hire company at the gust thresholds in the wind plan and on frame movement, and sends a post-storm report of which sites need a visit.

problem: Greenfield festivals hold toilet waste and urine in temporary steel or plastic tanks. A leak or overfill reaches watercourses. Event pollution plans require containment, yet tank levels are checked by eye, and in that case the EA's river sensors spotted the leak first.

current_workaround: Tanker crews dip tanks on their rounds, visual walk-rounds, and EA watercourse monitoring
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic level sensor on each holding tank, plus water-presence or float sensors in bunds and nearby drains. LTE-M, or a LoRaWAN gateway on site. Alerts on overfill, unexplained level drops (leaks) and liquid in bunds, and keeps an incident log for the EA.

problem: Hired accessible toilet units have emergency pull-cord alarms, but at festivals and outdoor events they only sound a local buzzer in a noisy field. Cords get tied up and batteries go flat. problem: Insurers' school fire guidance says bins should be locked away ~6–8 m from buildings, because arson often starts in bins pushed against walls. A school fire costs ~£ hundreds of thousands to millions and closes classrooms for months. RPA and local-authority insurers push schools on bin management.
who_suffers: Pupils displaced by fire; trust estates teams; insurers
buyer: Estates or site manager of a multi-academy trust or independent school, encouraged by the RPA or insurer
industry: Arson prevention on school estates
current_workaround: Bin compounds, chains and padlocks, and the site manager's evening checks
sensor_concept: Tilt, motion and temperature sensor inside each bin lid, plus BLE proximity to a gateway in the bin compound to detect a bin leaving it. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. Alerts out of hours when a bin is moved or heats up, and keeps a weekly 'bins secured' log for the insurer.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Multi-academy trusts can't prove each school's weekly fire-alarm test happened, and auditors and fire officers find the gaps
problem: BS 5839-1 and fire risk assessments expect a weekly call-point test recorded in the fire logbook. Across 10–40 schools, site staff skip weeks and logbooks go missing. The trust's central estates team only finds out at audit or after a fire-service visit, and enforcement notices and insurer challenges follow. A fire with a non-working alarm would leave the trust exposed.
who_suffers: Trust estates and compliance teams; site staff; pupils if an alarm fails
buyer: Head of estates or compliance manager of a multi-academy trust
industry: Fire safety compliance across multi-academy trusts
current_workaround: Paper fire logbooks, compliance software where staff tick boxes, and termly audits
sensor_concept: Plug-in acoustic sensor near a sounder that recognises the alarm tone pattern, or a volt-free relay input from the panel's sounder circuit. LTE-M. Auto-logs every test with its duration, flags missed weeks, and feeds a trust-wide dashboard.
notes: filtered: near-duplicate of R02-M-19 (weekly fire-alarm test records)

title: School boilers fail overnight and the head finds out at 7 am: cold classrooms, closures and emergency call-outs
problem: In older schools without a BMS, a boiler lockout or pump failure on a winter night leaves classrooms cold by morning. Schools send pupils home or close: each closure day costs ~£ thousands in staff time, hurts attendance and draws parent complaints. On top come emergency call-out rates.
who_suffers: Pupils and staff; heads managing closures; trust estates teams
buyer: Estates manager of a multi-academy trust, or the heating maintenance contractor that holds the schools' PPM contract
industry: School heating plant without a BMS
current_workaround: The caretaker arrives early to check, and the school calls out a contractor reactively
sensor_concept: Clamp-on pipe temperature sensors on flow and return, a current clamp on the circulation pump, and 2–3 classroom temperature tags. LTE-M. If flow temperature hasn't risen on schedule, the contractor gets an alert at 4 am. Also sends a monthly plant-health report.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Exam-paper secure rooms opened outside authorised windows, and centres can't show JCQ inspectors an access record
problem: JCQ rules require exam papers to be kept in a secure room or safe with restricted keyholders, and centres are inspected on this. Paper leaks or early openings lead to malpractice investigations, sanctions on the centre, and the cost of replacement papers for awarding bodies. Centres rely on handwritten logs.
who_suffers: Exams officers; heads; candidates if papers are compromised
buyer: School business manager or exams officer, or a MAT exams lead
industry: Examination centres in schools and colleges
current_workaround: Handwritten access log, keys held by the exams officer, and CCTV in some centres
sensor_concept: Reed contacts on the secure-room door and the safe, LTE-M. Alerts on openings outside timetabled windows, and exports a tamper-evident access log for the JCQ inspection.
notes: c4 strong: JCQ rules and the annual inspection. c8 trivial. c7 likely unserved. Weak on c1 and c5 (small budgets), so a long shot.

title: Radon sump fans in schools in radon Affected Areas fail silently, letting levels climb back above the action level
problem: Under the Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017, employers in radon Affected Areas must measure radon and act above 300 Bq/m³. Many schools fixed it with a radon sump and fan. If the fan fails or someone switches it off, levels rise again unnoticed until the next 3-month test, if one happens at all. HSE expects remediation to be kept working.
who_suffers: Staff and pupils exposed to radon; school H&S leads
buyer: Estates or H&S manager of a MAT or local-authority school estate in radon areas (e.g. Cornwall, Devon, Derbyshire, Northamptonshire)
industry: Radon remediation systems in schools
current_workaround: Occasional checks of a U-tube manometer on the pipe, and periodic retests with passive detectors
sensor_concept: Differential pressure switch or current clamp on the sump fan, with an optional low-cost radon sensor. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. Alerts on fan failure and issues a monthly 'system operating' certificate.
notes: c4 solid: IRR17 and UKHSA guidance. c8 very simple (a pressure switch). c7 likely unserved. c6 via radon remediation contractors. c1/c2 weak: the harm is long-term health, not a priced incident.

title: Spa and salon towels with massage oil self-heat in folded stacks overnight after a dryer cycle is cut short before cool-down
problem: Spa, salon, massage-clinic and hotel-spa towels carry treatment oils that low-temperature washes don't remove. Staff open the dryer mid-cycle or skip the cool-down to save time, then fold and stack warm towels. The stack self-heats and ignites after close (LFB Islington spa blaze; Chingford salon fire after towels left in a dryer overnight). A salon/spa fire typically costs ~£20k–£250k+ in damage and weeks of lost trading, and insurers question whether the business followed fire-service advice.
who_suffers: Spa/salon managers, therapists who do the laundry, hotel spa owners
buyer: Owner or Operations Manager of a multi-site salon/spa/hotel-spa group (bought through their laundry-equipment service contract)
industry: On-premises laundries in beauty salons, day spas, hotel spas and massage clinics
current_workaround: Fire-service leaflets and a notice telling staff to wash at 90°C and air towels before folding; nobody checks whether cool-down cycles finish
sensor_concept: CT current clamp on the dryer supply detects 'hot unload' events (heater stops and the cycle is aborted before cool-down) plus a LoRaWAN/LTE-M thermistor tag on the clean-towel shelf or trolley; alerts if stacked laundry exceeds ~45°C after close; monthly 'dryer discipline' report for the insurer
notes: Strong c10 (many fire-service warnings and named incidents) and c8 (clamp plus thermistor); c6 via laundry-equipment service firms (JLA, Forbes, Miele dealers); c7 likely unserved. Risk: c1 needs insured-loss figures.

title: Care-home tumble-dryer lint screens and exhaust ducts clog between cleans, causing laundry-room fires that force resident evacuations
problem: Care-home dryers run 10–14 h a day. Manufacturers require lint screens cleaned every cycle and ducts cleaned regularly, but night staff skip it, and lint-blocked dryers are a recurring cause of care-home laundry fires. A fire means a night evacuation of frail residents, ~£50k–£500k damage and closure to admissions, while the paper lint-cleaning sheet is blank.
who_suffers: Night care assistants/laundry staff, residents, registered manager
buyer: Group Estates/Maintenance Manager of a multi-home care group
industry: Care-home and nursing-home on-site laundries
current_workaround: Paper 'lint filter cleaned' tick-sheet on the laundry wall; an annual duct clean by a contractor if one is booked
sensor_concept: Low-cost differential-pressure (or exhaust-temperature) sensor in the dryer exhaust plus a current clamp; rising back-pressure flags a blocked screen or duct, and a pressure drop after cleaning logs each screen clean automatically; LTE-M alert and per-shift compliance log
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Care homes can't evidence that soiled and infected linen reached thermal-disinfection temperature (65°C/10 min or 71°C/3 min)
problem: HTM 01-04 and CQC infection-control expectations require foul and infected linen to be thermally disinfected. Staff pick the wrong programme, overload the machine or use domestic-grade machines, and nobody can prove a cycle reached temperature. Norovirus and C. diff outbreaks close homes to admissions, costing ~£1k+/day in lost fees, and CQC inspectors ask for evidence.
who_suffers: Laundry assistants, infection-prevention lead, residents
buyer: Registered Manager / Group Head of Quality & Compliance at a care group
industry: Care-home on-premises laundries (washer-extractors)
current_workaround: Trust in the machine programme; occasional thermal validation at service; no per-cycle record
sensor_concept: Clamp-on surface thermistor on the outer tub/drain plus a current clamp on the heater; firmware infers the time above 65/71°C per cycle and flags cycles that fail; LoRaWAN/LTE-M; monthly IPC audit report
notes: c4 strong (named HTM standard, CQC IPC); c2 daily; c6 via laundry-machine rental firms; c8 risk: an indicative rather than validated temperature, so it must be positioned as a screening log.

title: Kitchen extract ducts cleaned on a guessed TR19 interval because nobody records daily hours of use; insurers contest grease-fire claims
problem: BESA TR19 Grease sets duct-cleaning frequency by daily usage (~12-monthly for light, ~6-monthly for moderate, ~3-monthly for heavy use), and many insurers make TR19 compliance a policy condition. Restaurants under-declare usage to save on cleans, then a duct fire (~£100k+ damage and weeks closed) leads the insurer to argue the interval was wrong.
who_suffers: Restaurant/pub GMs, kitchen staff
buyer: Operations or Facilities Manager of a multi-site restaurant, pub or hotel group
industry: Commercial kitchens with canopy extract (restaurants, pubs, hotels, care-home kitchens)
current_workaround: Duct-cleaning contractor sets a schedule from a verbal estimate of hours; post-clean certificate; nothing measures real usage
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the extract-fan motor plus a duct thermistor near the canopy; LTE-M logs daily run-hours and heat load, computes the TR19-required interval, alerts when a clean is due or the fan fails, and stores evidence for the insurer
notes: c4 strong (TR19 named in insurer conditions); c6 strong (TR19 duct cleaners already visit and certify); c8 very simple; c7 likely unserved.

title: Independent washroom-service firms empty sanitary bins on fixed 4-weekly rounds: busy sites overflow and complain while quiet sites waste visits
problem: Sanitary and nappy bins are serviced on fixed cycles regardless of fill. Overflowing bins in busy offices, gyms and schools trigger complaints and contract cancellations (~£1k–£5k/yr each), while ~30–50% of visits to quiet sites empty half-full bins. Small washroom firms compete with Initial/PHS on price and service.
who_suffers: Route technicians, site facilities staff
buyer: Owner/Operations Director of an independent washroom-services company (bills per service)
industry: Washroom hygiene services (sanitary, nappy, clinical-offensive waste bins)
current_workaround: Fixed-frequency rounds; ad-hoc extra visits after complaints; paper or app service sheets
sensor_concept: Time-of-flight fill sensor in the bin lid plus NB-IoT/LoRaWAN; fill dashboard, route optimisation and proof-of-service log for customer and duty-of-care records
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Contract cleaners can't prove wet-floor signs were out during mopping, so supermarket and shopping-centre slip claims settle
problem: Slip claims against retailers and their cleaning contractors typically settle at ~£3k–£25k+ each plus legal costs. The defence depends on proving a reasonable cleaning-and-signage system was operating at the time of the fall. Paper cleaning logs are easily challenged, and contractors carry the claim or the excess under indemnity clauses.
who_suffers: Cleaning operatives, site supervisors, claims handlers
buyer: Operations Director / Head of Risk & Insurance at a contract-cleaning company
industry: Contract cleaning of supermarkets, shopping centres, stations and hospitals
current_workaround: Paper cleaning logs on the wall, CCTV requests that often arrive after footage is overwritten, and the insurer settles
sensor_concept: Accelerometer/tilt tag inside A-frame wet-floor signs logs deployed and folded times; BLE zone beacons give location; LoRaWAN/LTE-M uplink; claims-defence report matching signage to the cleaning schedule and incident time
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Restaurant grease traps overfill between fixed pump-outs; water companies recharge sewer-blockage costs and kitchens flood with backed-up waste
problem: Grease traps and grease-removal units are emptied on fixed contractor schedules. Busy weeks overfill them, fats pass to the sewer and blockages follow. Water companies recharge clearance costs (~£1k–£10k+), can prosecute under the Water Industry Act s111, and a backed-up trap can close a kitchen for days.
who_suffers: Kitchen managers, restaurant GMs
buyer: Facilities Manager of a multi-site restaurant/takeaway/QSR group
industry: Commercial-kitchen grease-trap servicing
current_workaround: Fixed monthly or quarterly pump-outs by a grease-trap contractor; visual checks by kitchen staff
sensor_concept: Float level switch in the trap outlet chamber (no probe in the grease layer) plus LTE-M; high-level alert before overflow, pump-out events logged as FOG-compliance evidence for the water company
notes: filtered: duplicate of R02-B-01 (grease traps)

title: Accessible-toilet emergency pull cords tied up or cut short by cleaners, leaving fallen disabled users unable to raise the alarm
problem: Approved Document M and BS 8300 require the alarm cord to reach the floor. Cleaners routinely loop the cords up out of the way (campaigns such as the 'Red Cord Card'), and people who fall lie undiscovered for long periods. Venues face Equality Act complaints, reputational damage and injury claims.
who_suffers: Disabled toilet users, venue staff
buyer: Facilities Manager of a shopping centre, station operator or motorway-services group
industry: Accessible toilets and Changing Places facilities in public venues
current_workaround: Occasional manager walk-rounds; awareness cards handed to staff; weekly alarm tests rarely recorded
sensor_concept: Tilt/reed tag on the bottom bangle of the pull cord detects when it is lifted or looped; LoRaWAN uplink; alert to the cleaning supervisor; weekly test log
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Independent funeral homes' body fridges fail over a weekend with no temperature log, ahead of statutory inspection in England and Scotland
problem: After the Legacy (Hull) scandal and the Fuller Inquiry's call for statutory regulation, councils have run mass inspections of funeral premises, and Scotland already has an Inspector of Funeral Directors and a statutory code. A body-store failure over a bank holiday leaves the deceased deteriorating, viewings cancelled and the family complaining, with goodwill refunds and reputational loss of ~£2k–£10k+ per case; independents have no record to show an inspector.
who_suffers: Funeral directors, bereaved families, mortuary staff
buyer: Owner of an independent funeral home, or Head of Care/Operations at a mid-size funeral group
industry: Independent funeral directors' mortuaries/body stores
current_workaround: Glance at the fridge display when opening up; handwritten temperature sheet if any; refrigeration engineer once a year
sensor_concept: LoRaWAN/LTE-M temperature probe per body store plus a door reed; out-of-hours alert by phone and SMS; daily signed-off log and an inspector-ready monthly report
notes: c4 is rising fast (Fuller Inquiry, Scottish code, council inspections) and c10 strong (national news); c6 via mortuary refrigeration servicers and NAFD/SAIF buying schemes; c7 risk from generic fridge loggers, so the niche report is the differentiator.

title: No record of where each deceased is or how long they spent out of refrigeration (viewing, dressing, embalming): wrong-body and condition complaints
problem: Deceased are moved between body store, preparation room and chapel of rest, sometimes left in a warm chapel overnight. Misidentification or deterioration complaints lead to compensation (~£1k–£10k+), trade-association discipline and press coverage, and inspection regimes now ask for chain-of-custody records.
who_suffers: Funeral arrangers and bearers, bereaved families
buyer: Compliance/Care Standards Manager at a multi-branch funeral group, or the independent owner
industry: Funeral-home care centres and chapels of rest
current_workaround: Paper ID bracelets and a whiteboard; staff memory
sensor_concept: BLE tag fixed to each body tray or coffin (assigned at admission) plus gateways in the body store, prep room and chapel; logs location and cumulative time out of cold, with alerts for any deceased out of refrigeration beyond ~X hours or overnight
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Pet crematoria collect from vets' carcass freezers on fixed weekly rounds: some freezers overflow or fail between visits, others are half-empty
problem: Vet practices hold deceased pets in chest freezers until the pet-crematorium van calls. Full or failed freezers mean decomposing animals, upset owners whose individual cremation is compromised, refunds and lost vet accounts (a practice account is worth ~£5k–£30k/yr to the crematorium). Meanwhile fixed rounds waste driver hours on near-empty freezers. Storage and transport fall under the Animal By-Products Regulations.
who_suffers: Vet nurses, crematorium drivers, pet owners
buyer: Operations/Logistics Manager of a pet crematorium group
industry: Pet cremation services collecting from veterinary practices
current_workaround: Fixed weekly or fortnightly rounds; vets phone when full; drivers find failed freezers on arrival

title: Out-of-hours access to funeral-home mortuaries isn't logged, the gap the Fuller Inquiry exposed
problem: The Fuller Inquiry showed that unrestricted, unlogged mortuary access lets abuse of the deceased go undetected for years. Its funeral-sector phase urges access control and audit. Funeral homes mostly rely on a shared key and an intruder alarm, so they can't say who entered the body store at 2 am. The exposure is criminal, civil-claim and reputational.

title: Embalming-room downdraft extraction not running during embalming: formaldehyde exposure with no record between 14-month LEV tests
problem: Embalmers work with formaldehyde-based fluids under a COSHH workplace exposure limit that is under review. LEV must be thoroughly examined every 14 months. Fans are switched off for noise, or filters clog, and nobody knows whether extraction ran during each embalming. HSE enforcement, ill-health claims and failed audits follow.

problem: Home wakes and home funerals (common in several faith and cultural communities, and growing) use cooling plates or blankets supplied by the funeral director. problem: Removal contractors and funeral directors on coroner and hospital contracts are meant to take the deceased directly to refrigerated storage. title: Bath-water temperature not checked and recorded before every assisted bath: scalding deaths, falsified logs and six- to seven-figure fines
problem: HSE guidance requires care homes to control bath water to ≤44°C and to check it before each bath. Prosecutions follow scalds: Salutem was fined £100k after staff didn't check the water; Aster Healthcare was fined £1.04m for corporate manslaughter, with temperature records found falsified; Greencroft was fined after a resident died of bath burns. Paper bath-temperature logs are routinely blank or invented.

current_workaround: Handheld bath thermometer plus a paper bath-temperature chart; annual TMV service
sensor_concept: Waterproof BLE/LoRaWAN dip thermometer that logs a reading tied to room and resident (NFC tap) before each bath, plus a clamp thermistor on the bath hot feed after the TMV that alerts if water above 44°C reaches the outlet; tamper-proof bath log for CQC

title: Smouldering fires after hot works on historic roofs: the 60-minute fire watch is unprovable and the roof void is unwatched overnight
problem: Lead-roofing, plumbing and torch-on work on historic buildings is a classic cause of catastrophic heritage fires (Uppark, 1989, was started by a contractor's blowlamp on the roof). The Joint Code of Practice on fire prevention on construction sites and insurers' hot-work permits require at least 60 minutes of fire watch after work stops, with later checks. In a void of dry historic timber, though, a smoulder can break out hours later after the site is locked. Losses run to £m, and a contractor that cannot show the permit conditions were met faces uninsured liability.
who_suffers: Owners of heritage buildings, conservation contractors and their insurers
buyer: Contracts Manager / Managing Director of a heritage roofing, leadwork or conservation contractor
industry: Conservation roofing, leadwork and building contractors working on listed buildings, churches and historic houses
current_workaround: Paper hot-work permits, operatives standing fire watch for an hour, sometimes temporary site fire alarms. FM-approved remote fire-watch systems exist but are camera-based, US/industrial and costly.
sensor_concept: Clip-on battery node with an 8x8 thermopile array (AMG8833-class, not a camera) aimed at the work area, plus a rate-of-rise heat sensor and an optical smoke sensor. LTE-M. Logs the 60-minute watch, then keeps monitoring for 12–24 hours after works, alerting the site manager and keyholder. Hired per day, with a permit-compliance PDF.
notes: c1: £m heritage fire losses. c4: JCOP and insurer hot-work conditions. c5: the contractor owns permit compliance and liability. c6: heritage insurers and roofing/scaffold suppliers already serve these jobs. c7: incumbents are camera-based enterprise kit. c8: thermopile, smoke and LTE-M are cheap.

title: Bronze sculptures, lead statues and stone urns lifted from country-house gardens and sculpture parks overnight
problem: Outdoor statuary is stolen to order or for scrap. A Henry Moore bronze valued at ~£3m was taken from the Henry Moore Foundation in 2005 and is believed to have been melted down. Lead garden statues and antique urns (~£5k–£100k each) regularly vanish from estates. Specialist fine-art and heritage insurers impose security conditions on outdoor works, but grounds are far too large for conventional intruder alarms.
who_suffers: Owners of historic houses and estates, sculpture parks and garden-antiques dealers; their insurers
buyer: Estate Manager / Owner of a privately owned historic house run as a visitor or wedding business, or Collections Manager of a commercial sculpture park
industry: Privately owned historic houses, sculpture parks and garden-antiques dealers
current_workaround: Bolting or anchoring in concrete, forensic marking, occasional CCTV near the house, and night patrols on larger estates.
sensor_concept: Puck bonded under or inside the plinth with an accelerometer/tilt sensor to detect lifting, cutting or tilting. LoRaWAN to an estate gateway, or LTE-M. Instant alerts to keyholders via an alarm-receiving centre, plus a monthly status report for the insurer.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Fine-art vans left unattended at services or loading bays, breaching loan conditions and losing theft cover
problem: Museum loan agreements, Government Indemnity Scheme conditions and fine-art transit policies typically require works in transit to travel in alarmed, climate-controlled vehicles that are never left unattended, usually with two crew. Thefts from vans parked at services or outside venues can involve ~£50k to £m of objects and are refused or disputed if the vehicle was left. Lenders also demand a journey report, which the shipper reconstructs from memory and paper.
who_suffers: Lending museums and collectors, fine-art shippers and couriers
buyer: Operations Director / Head of Transport at a fine-art logistics company
industry: Fine-art shipping and handling firms serving museums, galleries and auction houses
current_workaround: Two-person crews, generic vehicle trackers, separate temperature/RH loggers in the cargo bay and paper courier reports.
sensor_concept: Cab occupancy sensor (mmWave radar/PIR), cargo-door reed contacts, cargo-bay temperature/RH and shock sensors, and GPS. LTE-M. Alert if the cab is empty with the engine off while a loan is aboard. Automatic per-journey compliance report (attended time, door openings, climate) for lenders and insurers.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Overfired wood-burners and unswept flues set thatched holiday cottages and pubs alight
problem: Fire services attribute most thatch fires to chimneys and wood-burners: sparks, or a flue run too hot, ignite the thatch. A thatch fire typically costs ~£250k–£1m+ and can destroy a listed building. Specialist thatch insurers require annual sweeping, spark arrestors and sensible use. Owners of holiday lets and pubs, however, cannot see how hard guests and staff run the stove.
who_suffers: Owners of thatched holiday lets and pubs; guests; insurers
buyer: Owner/Operator of a thatched holiday-let portfolio, or Estates Manager at a pub company with thatched pubs
industry: Thatched listed holiday cottages, pubs and inns
current_workaround: Annual chimney sweep certificate, spark arrestor, house rules for guests, and magnetic stove-pipe thermometers that nobody reads.
sensor_concept: Thermocouple strap on the flue pipe (MAX31855-class interface) with LTE-M. Alerts on overfiring and chimney-fire temperature signatures, counts burn hours so the sweep is booked on actual usage, and produces an insurer report of sweeping and safe use.
notes: c1: high loss per fire. c4: insurer sweeping conditions. c6: chimney sweeps (HETAS/NACS) visit yearly, and thatch insurers/brokers could subsidise. c8: thermocouple plus cellular is cheap. c5 is weaker for single-cottage owners.

title: Listed buildings next to basement digs and demolitions: party-wall awards demand crack and tilt readings taken by hand
problem: Party-wall awards and planning conditions for works next to listed or historic buildings commonly require crack and tilt monitoring of the neighbour for the duration of the works. Surveyors visit monthly or fortnightly to read tell-tale gauges and level points (~£200–£500 a visit). Movement between visits goes unseen, and damage claims (~£10k–£100k+) are argued over without a continuous record.
who_suffers: Owners of the adjoining listed building; the developer; the basement or demolition contractor
buyer: Project Manager at a basement/refurbishment contractor, or the developer paying for monitoring under the party-wall award
industry: Basement construction and refurbishment next to listed terraces and heritage buildings (London and historic towns)
current_workaround: Manual tell-tale and precise-levelling readings by monitoring surveyors. Wireless structural monitoring (tiltmeters, crack meters) is used only on large projects.
sensor_concept: Battery crack-displacement sensor (linear potentiometer bridging the crack) plus a MEMS tilt sensor on the façade. LoRaWAN/LTE-M, reading hourly. Alerts at the trigger levels set in the award, and a monthly report for both party-wall surveyors.
notes: c2: monthly duty. c3: paid surveyor visits. c4: award or planning condition. c5: contractor/developer pays. c6: party-wall surveyors and monitoring firms already visit. c7: enterprise wireless monitoring is priced for major projects. c8: potentiometer plus MEMS tilt.

title: Temporary roofs over historic buildings under restoration lift or overflow in storms, pouring rain onto exposed interiors
problem: When a historic roof is stripped for re-leading or re-slating, a scaffold temporary roof or sheeting protects the interior for months. In gales the sheets lift or temporary gutters overflow, and water reaches decorative plaster ceilings, panelling and contents (~£50k–£500k+ claims under works or existing-structures insurance). Temporary works are inspected weekly and after storms, but the damage happens overnight.
who_suffers: Owners of historic buildings, conservation main contractors and scaffold contractors
buyer: Contracts Manager at a heritage main contractor, or at the scaffold contractor providing the temporary roof
industry: Heritage restoration projects under scaffold temporary roofs
current_workaround: Weekly scaffold inspections, after-storm visits, and buckets and polythene.
sensor_concept: Hire kit: water-presence sensors at low points on exposed ceilings and attic floors, float switches in temporary gutters, and accelerometer/tilt nodes on temporary roof sheets, plus a site anemometer. LTE-M. Storm alerts to the contractor's on-call manager, with time-stamped evidence for insurers.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Frost kills fresh lime mortar and plaster on winter heritage repairs, and the contractor can't show it was protected
problem: Lime pointing, render and plaster on listed buildings must be protected from frost and rapid drying while they cure, and specifications typically forbid work, or demand protection, below ~5°C. One frosty night under inadequate hessian can blow fresh lime work, which then has to be raked out and redone (~£5k–£50k on a large elevation). Clients and conservation officers then dispute who pays, because nobody recorded conditions at the wall face overnight.
who_suffers: Heritage masonry and plastering contractors; building owners
buyer: Contracts Manager / Owner of a heritage masonry, lime-plastering or conservation contractor
industry: Conservation masonry and lime-plastering contractors on listed buildings and churches
current_workaround: Weather forecasts, hessian and polythene sheeting, occasional site heaters and morning inspections, with nothing recorded overnight.
sensor_concept: Clip-on scaffold nodes with an air temperature/RH sensor and a contact thermistor on the wall face behind the sheeting. LTE-M, battery powered, as hire kits. Frost-risk alert in the evening, to add protection or heaters, and a time-stamped curing-conditions record per elevation for the client and conservation officer.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Livery-yard horses escape onto roads through gates left open by liveries or through dead electric fencing
problem: On DIY and part-livery yards dozens of owners use the same field and yard gates, and electric fences short out on wet grass or fallen branches. Loose horses on roads cause collisions; keepers can be held strictly liable under the Animals Act 1971, and claims run to ~£100k–£1m+ (injuries, vehicles, horses destroyed). Yard owners are expected to check fencing and gates daily, and their liability insurers ask about it.
who_suffers: Yard owners, horse owners and motorists
buyer: Owner/Proprietor of a commercial livery yard or equestrian centre (20–80 horses)
industry: Commercial livery yards and equestrian centres
current_workaround: 'Shut the gate' signs, padlocks and yard rules, walking fence lines daily with a fence tester, and Wi-Fi energisers only near the house.
sensor_concept: Gate nodes with reed/tilt sensors (alert if open more than 5 minutes) and electric-fence line monitors (pulse detection through a high-voltage divider) at the far end of each paddock line. LoRaWAN gateway at the yard, or LTE-M nodes. Alerts to the yard manager's phone, plus a daily fence/gate check record for insurers.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: A stabled horse stops drinking overnight and colic is only noticed at morning feed: £5k–£10k surgery or a dead horse
problem: A drop in water intake is one of the earliest signs of colic, but automatic drinkers give staff no idea how much each horse drank. Colic surgery costs ~£5k–£10k and is among the largest categories of equine insurance claim. At racing and competition yards, a horse lost or off work costs far more. Welfare codes expect water to be checked at least twice daily.
who_suffers: Horses, owners, yard managers and equine insurers
buyer: Head Lad / Yard Manager at a racing yard, or Proprietor of a full-livery or competition yard
industry: Racing yards and full-livery or competition yards fitted with automatic drinkers
current_workaround: Buckets instead of automatic drinkers so staff can eyeball intake, plus evening and late-night checks. A couple of small vendors (HydraSure, Cascada) sell their own smart drinkers rather than retrofits for existing fittings.
sensor_concept: Inline Hall-effect pulse flow meter (~£5) on each stable drinker feed with a LoRaWAN node. Builds a per-horse daily intake baseline and alerts on a sharp overnight drop or no flow (frozen or blocked drinker). Weekly intake report for vets and owners.
notes: c1: colic surgery cost. c2: daily. c5: yard proprietor or head lad. c6: equine vets visit yards weekly, and equine insurers pay the colic claims. c8: flow meter plus LPWAN. c7: two small own-hardware incumbents leave a retrofit gap.

title: Commercial horse transporters can't evidence in-transit temperatures and journeys, and horses arrive with shipping fever
problem: Heat and poor air in a closed horse lorry cause heat stress and transport-associated pleuropneumonia ('shipping fever') in horses worth ~£20k to £1m+. Animal transport rules (Regulation (EC) 1/2005 as retained, WATO 2006) require transporter authorisation and, for long journeys of unregistered horses, temperature monitoring, recording and navigation records. Owners and insurers of registered sport horses and racehorses increasingly expect the same evidence. Many lorries have only a cab thermometer.
who_suffers: Horses and owners; commercial transporters and their insurers
buyer: Owner/Managing Director of a commercial horse transport company (Type 1/Type 2 authorised)
industry: Commercial equine transport (racing, sport-horse and bloodstock shipping)
current_workaround: Cab dial thermometers, paper journey logs and driver judgement on vents. Integrated systems come only on new high-end lorries.
sensor_concept: Temperature/humidity sensors at horse head height in each bay, an accelerometer on partitions (horse down or scrambling) and GPS. LTE-M. Driver alerts in the cab via a phone app, plus an automatic journey log and temperature record for APHA, export paperwork and owners.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Horseboxes run over their plated weight once horses and kit are aboard, bringing DVSA prohibitions, fines and void insurance
problem: 3.5t and 7.5t horseboxes are easily overloaded once horses, water, tack and living kit are aboard. DVSA roadside checks issue prohibitions and fines, and an overweight vehicle can invalidate insurance after a crash. Horsebox hire firms and commercial transporters carry the operator liability but cannot see what hirers or drivers load.
who_suffers: Horsebox hire firms, commercial transporters, drivers and horses
buyer: Owner of a horsebox hire business, or Transport Manager of a commercial equine transporter
industry: Horsebox hire and commercial equine transport (3.5t–7.5t vehicles)
current_workaround: Weighbridge visits when convenient, payload tables, and warnings in the hire T&Cs.
sensor_concept: Ride-height distance sensors (ToF/ultrasonic) between chassis and axle, calibrated once at a weighbridge, plus LTE-M/GPS. In-cab and app warning when the estimated gross weight exceeds the plate, and a trip-level weight record for hire disputes and DVSA.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Stable-block fires start at night on unmanned yards, where dust-triggered false alarms mean smoke alarms get unplugged
problem: Electrical faults, heaters, rug dryers, hay and bedding start stable fires that kill horses and destroy buildings (~£50k–£500k+ per fire). Domestic smoke detectors false-alarm constantly in dusty stables and get removed, and many yards have nobody on site overnight. Yard insurers and equine welfare bodies recommend detection suited to stables.
who_suffers: Horses, yard owners, livery clients and insurers
buyer: Proprietor of a livery or competition yard, or racing Yard Manager
industry: Livery, racing and competition yards with timber or barn stabling
current_workaround: No detection, or wired heat detectors only in large new barns; staff night checks; CCTV.
sensor_concept: Node in each stable aisle combining a rate-of-rise heat sensor and an electrochemical CO sensor (CO detects smouldering bedding without dust false alarms). LoRaWAN or LTE-M, battery powered. Escalating phone alerts to on-call staff and neighbours, plus a monthly self-test record for insurers.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Horse walkers keep turning when a horse slips or is cast, and the racing yard finds the injury when staff come back
problem: Racing and competition yards put 4–6 horses at a time on mechanical horse walkers, often left for 30–60 minutes. If a horse slips, turns or is cast against a panel, the walker keeps pushing, causing injuries and occasionally deaths (vet bills ~£2k–£10k, and lost racehorse value far beyond that).
who_suffers: Horses, trainers and owners
buyer: Racehorse Trainer / Yard Manager
industry: Racing and competition yards using mechanical horse walkers
current_workaround: Stable staff checking periodically, CCTV, and built-in overload trips on some newer walkers.
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the walker drive motor (torque spike when a horse resists or is down) plus an accelerometer on a divider panel (impacts). LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Immediate phone alert, and a run log for every session.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Buried pipes to paddock troughs leak for months at studs and livery yards: £5k+ water bills and dry troughs
problem: Studs and large livery yards run hundreds of metres of buried alkathene to field troughs. A split pipe or stuck ballcock can lose tens of cubic metres a day unnoticed, producing water bills of ~£5k–£20k before the next meter read, while horses in that field may be left without water. Non-household water retailers grant leak allowances only on proof of prompt repair.
who_suffers: Stud and yard owners; horses
buyer: Owner / Stud Manager of a stud farm or large livery yard
industry: Stud farms, large livery yards and equestrian centres with field troughs
current_workaround: Quarterly or estimated bills, walking the fields, and isolating sections to find leaks.
sensor_concept: Pulse reader clipped onto the existing water meter (reed or magnetometer pick-up), LTE-M/LoRaWAN. Night-flow leak detection, daily consumption trend and spike alerts, with optional trough float switches in remote fields.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Dental suction motors and compressors fail mid-list in older practices, cancelling whole days of patients
problem: A failed wet-suction motor, compressor or air dryer stops every surgery in the practice. For a 4–6 chair practice a lost day is ~£5k–£10k of production, plus handpiece damage from wet air. Most practice compressors are pressure systems needing a PSSR written scheme and daily draining, and HTM 01-05 requires daily suction cleaning, but all these checks are manual. OEM remote monitoring (Dürr VistaSoft Monitor, DentalEZ Aeras, Air Techniques) only covers the maker's own newer units, not the mixed legacy plant in most UK practices.
who_suffers: Dentists, nurses and patients; the practice owner
buyer: Practice Owner/Principal, or Facilities/Compliance Manager at a dental group (e.g. Bupa Dental Care, mydentist, Portman, Rodericks)
industry: General dental practices with plant-room compressors and suction units
current_workaround: Annual service and PSSR inspection by independent dental engineers, nurses draining compressors and cleaning suction daily, and emergency call-outs.
sensor_concept: Current clamps on suction and compressor motors (duty cycle, start counts, overcurrent), a pressure transducer on the receiver, and temperature/humidity in the plant cupboard. LTE-M. Alerts on air leaks (rising duty cycle), overheating and missed drains, plus usage-based service tickets to the engineer.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Vet anaesthetic scavenging left off or failing exposes nurses to isoflurane between annual tests
problem: Vet practices run general anaesthetics daily. Active scavenging (AGSS) fans get switched off, ducts disconnect or flows drop, exposing nurses, including pregnant staff, to isoflurane above the workplace exposure limit. COSHH requires effective control, periodic thorough examination of the system and exposure monitoring, and RCVS Practice Standards assessors check it. Personal dosimetry is done once a year at best.
who_suffers: Veterinary nurses and surgeons; practice owners
buyer: Clinical Director / Group Health & Safety Manager at a veterinary group (e.g. IVC Evidensia, CVS, Medivet, Linnaeus)
industry: Small-animal veterinary practices and hospitals
current_workaround: Annual AGSS/LEV test by a contractor, annual personal badge sampling, and nurses glancing at the flow indicator.
sensor_concept: Differential pressure sensor in the scavenging duct, a current clamp on the AGSS fan, and an oxygen-flowmeter on/off sensor at the anaesthetic machine to detect 'GA in progress'. LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Alert when anaesthesia runs with scavenging off or under-flowing, and a monthly COSHH record per theatre.
notes: c2: daily GA. c4: COSHH and RCVS PSS. c5: vet group H&S has budget. c6: anaesthetic-machine and AGSS service engineers visit annually. c8: DP sensor plus clamp. c1 is weak (claims are rare).

title: Second-hand MRI scanners at vet referral centres: a chiller or cold-head compressor trips at the weekend and the helium boils off
problem: Veterinary referral hospitals often run refurbished superconducting MRI systems without the manufacturer's remote-monitoring service contract. If the chiller or cold-head compressor stops over a weekend (power blip, water-flow fault), liquid helium boils off and the magnet can quench. Helium refill and re-ramping cost ~£30k–£100k+, and the scanner is out of action for days to weeks while referrals go elsewhere.
who_suffers: Referral hospital clinicians and owners; patients awaiting scans
buyer: Hospital Director / Head of Diagnostic Imaging at a veterinary referral centre or vet group
industry: Veterinary referral hospitals running MRI
current_workaround: Local compressor alarm lamps, staff checks on weekdays, and third-party service contracts with periodic visits.
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the cold-head compressor, temperature sensors on chilled-water flow and return, a flow switch and mains-loss detection, all installed outside the RF-shielded room. LTE-M. Immediate alerts to on-call staff and the service engineer, plus a run log for the service contract.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Controlled-drug cabinets in vet and dental-sedation practices are opened with no record that matches the register
problem: Ketamine, methadone and midazolam go missing from practice CD cabinets. Stock is reconciled against the register only periodically, so diversion surfaces weeks later and leads to RCVS/GDC proceedings, police involvement and dismissals. Practices must keep CDs in a locked cabinet with a running register, and practice-standards and CQC inspectors check stock and records.
who_suffers: Practice owners and clinical directors; honest staff under suspicion
buyer: Clinical Director / Compliance Manager at a veterinary or dental group
industry: Veterinary practices and dental practices offering IV sedation
current_workaround: Key-holder logs, weekly or monthly stock checks, and CCTV in some dispensaries. Electronic CD cabinets cost thousands.
sensor_concept: Reed contact on the CD cabinet door, an accelerometer for forced entry, and an optional NFC fob tap by the person opening it. LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Time-stamped opening log reconciled against register entries, with alerts for out-of-hours or unrecorded openings.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Vet practices run out of oxygen mid-anaesthetic because nobody saw the cylinder bank empty
problem: Small-animal practices run every general anaesthetic on oxygen from cylinders on the machine or a small manifold. When the duty cylinder empties and the reserve is low or shut, nurses scramble mid-procedure. The result is a patient-safety incident and potential negligence claim (~£2k–£20k), plus emergency deliveries. Practice standards require the anaesthetic machine and gas supply to be checked before each list.
who_suffers: Vet nurses, surgeons and patients
buyer: Practice Manager / Clinical Director at an independent practice or vet group
industry: Small-animal veterinary practices using cylinder oxygen
current_workaround: Pre-list machine checks, reading gauges by eye, and keeping spare cylinders.
sensor_concept: Load-cell cradle under each cylinder estimating contents by weight, so nothing is fitted to the medical gas line, plus LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Low-contents and reorder alerts, and a pre-list check record per theatre.
notes: c2: daily use. c6: gas suppliers deliver weekly and could bundle it. c8: load cell plus LPWAN. c1 and c4 are moderate.

title: Hourly metal-detector tests at small food producers are back-filled on paper, and a detector that failed its test keeps running
problem: HACCP and BRCGS/SALSA require metal detectors to be challenged with ferrous, non-ferrous and stainless test pieces at set intervals (typically hourly, at start-up and at changeovers), with rejects confirmed into a locked bin. In small factories tests are skipped on busy shifts and ticked later, and auditors frequently raise non-conformities. A metal-contamination recall costs a small producer ~£20k–£200k plus possible delisting. Digital self-test systems come only with new premium detectors.
who_suffers: Line operators, technical managers, and the business that recalls
buyer: Technical Manager / Owner of an SME food manufacturer (SALSA or BRCGS certified)
industry: SME bakeries, ready-meal, snack, meat and confectionery producers with legacy metal detectors
current_workaround: Paper hourly test sheets, supervisor sign-off, and annual detector validation by the service engineer.
sensor_concept: Retrofit box wired to the detector's dry-contact outputs (detect/reject/fault). NFC-tagged test wands are read at the aperture so each test-piece type is logged, an IR beam in the reject bin confirms rejects arrive, and a reed contact sits on the bin lock. LoRaWAN/NB-IoT. Missed-test alerts to the supervisor, and an audit-ready CCP record.
notes: c2: hourly duty. c3: labour-heavy paper checks. c4: HACCP/BRCGS/SALSA CCP records. c5: technical manager owns audit and recall. c6: detector service engineers visit yearly. c7: OEM digital testing only on new high-end units. c8: contacts, NFC and IR beam.

title: High-care rooms lose positive air pressure unnoticed between once-a-shift gauge readings, raising Listeria risk in ready-to-eat food
problem: Ready-to-eat producers (sandwiches, salads, cooked meats) must keep high-care/high-risk areas supplied with filtered air at positive pressure relative to low-care areas, under BRCGS high-risk zone requirements. A failed fan, clogged filter or propped door reverses the airflow. Pressure is read off a dial gauge once a shift. Listeria outbreaks linked to RTE producers, such as the 2019 hospital-sandwich outbreak, led to closures and recalls costing £100ks.
who_suffers: Consumers (especially vulnerable ones), technical teams and the producer
buyer: Technical / Hygiene Manager at an SME ready-to-eat food manufacturer
industry: Chilled ready-to-eat producers: sandwiches, salads, cooked meats and ready meals
current_workaround: Daily manual gauge readings on paper and quarterly air-handling service. BMS monitoring exists only on large sites.
sensor_concept: Digital differential-pressure sensor (Sensirion SDP-class) across each high-care wall or door, plus door contacts. LoRaWAN. Alarm if the differential collapses for more than N minutes, and a continuous record for BRCGS auditors and EHOs.
notes: c2/c3: daily manual readings. c4: BRCGS high-risk requirements. c5: technical manager. c6: HVAC maintainers visit quarterly. c8: cheap DP sensor. c1 is indirect (via outbreak risk).

title: Fryer and oven extract ducts in food factories are cleaned on a guessed schedule, and insurers refuse fire claims without TR19 proof
problem: Grease builds up in extract ductwork over frying ranges, ovens and smokehouses. TR19 Grease (BESA) sets cleaning frequency by hours of use, and insurers make TR19 cleaning a policy condition. One insurer reportedly refused a ~£2m hotel fire claim for lack of deep-clean records, and ombudsman cases turn on fryer-duct cleaning. Food factories running two or three shifts slip past the interval because nobody tracks actual usage hours.
who_suffers: Factory owners, engineering managers and insurers
buyer: Engineering Manager / Owner of an SME food manufacturer with frying, roasting or baking lines
industry: Food manufacturers with fryer, oven and smokehouse extract systems (snacks, fried foods, bakery, meat)
current_workaround: Fixed-interval TR19 cleans by a duct-hygiene contractor (~£500–£3k per clean) with certificates on file, but no record of real usage hours.
sensor_concept: Current clamp or vibration sensor on each extract fan for run-hours, plus a duct-surface temperature sensor as an over-temperature/fire precursor. LTE-M/LoRaWAN. Calculates the TR19 cleaning due date from actual hours and books the contractor, alerts on duct over-temperature, and keeps an insurer-ready history.
notes: filtered: near-duplicate of R02-C-04 (extract duct cleaning interval)

title: Knife sterilisers in meat cutting plants drift below 82°C mid-shift, triggering FSA audit non-compliances
problem: Approved meat establishments must provide tool sterilisers supplied with water at not less than 82°C, or an equivalent system. Kettles get topped up with cold water, elements fail or units are switched off. Official veterinarians record the shortfall, which affects the plant's audit outcome, audit frequency and FSA charges. After E. coli or Salmonella findings, product is held (~£5k–£50k). Operators currently dip a thermometer a few times a shift.
who_suffers: Plant operators, technical managers and consumers
buyer: Technical Manager / Plant Manager of an FSA-approved cutting plant or small abattoir
industry: FSA-approved meat cutting plants, small abattoirs and game-handling establishments
current_workaround: Manual thermometer checks recorded on paper 2–4 times a shift, plus OV spot checks.
sensor_concept: Sealed stainless temperature probe clipped into each steriliser, with LoRaWAN, since steel-clad cold rooms make Wi-Fi unreliable. Alert below 82°C for more than N minutes, and a per-steriliser HACCP record for the OV and FSA audit.
notes: c2: several checks per shift. c4: legal temperature with an audit regime. c5: plant technical manager. c6: hygiene-chemical suppliers and plant engineers visit weekly. c8: simple immersion temperature probe. c1 is moderate.

title: Small dairies' batch-pasteuriser chart recorders jam or run out of ink, so the batch can't be released
problem: Farm dairies, ice-cream makers and cheesemakers pasteurising in vats must be able to show each batch reached time and temperature, normally via an automatic recorder. Paper chart recorders jam, lose pens or drift, and a batch without a valid record has to be held or discarded (~£1k–£5k a batch). Missing records are a standard EHO/FSA finding. Paperless recorders cost ~£1k+ installed and still need someone to watch them.
who_suffers: Dairy owners, cheesemakers and ice-cream makers
buyer: Owner/Operator of an on-farm dairy, artisan cheesemaker or ice-cream manufacturer
industry: On-farm dairies and artisan cheese and ice-cream producers using batch (vat) pasteurisation
current_workaround: Circular paper chart recorders, manual thermometer reads written up afterwards, and annual calibration.
sensor_concept: Calibrated PT100 probe in the vat thermowell plus agitator current sensing, LTE-M. Time-at-temperature record per batch, a real-time alert if holding temperature drops, and a signed digital batch chart for EHOs and customers.
notes: c4: recording requirement and inspections. c2: every batch. c5: owner-operator. c6: dairy equipment engineers and dairy consultants. c8: needs a traceable-calibrated PT100 (moderate). c7: paperless recorders exist but aren't cloud-connected or cheap.

title: Artisan smokehouse kilns overheat or flare overnight, causing smokery fires and leaving cold-smoked fish with no temperature record
problem: Smoke generators and wood-fired kilns run unattended overnight. Sawdust flare-ups and grease deposits cause smokehouse fires that can destroy premises (~£100k+). Cold-smoked salmon must be held below ~30°C during smoking to manage Listeria and C. botulinum risk, with records expected in the HACCP plan. Older and home-built kilns have no logging.
who_suffers: Smokery owners, staff and consumers
buyer: Owner/Operator of an artisan smokehouse or small smoked-fish/meat processor
industry: Artisan smokeries and small smoked fish, meat and cheese producers
current_workaround: Dial thermometers, staff checking kilns at night, and paper HACCP logs.
sensor_concept: Thermocouples in the kiln chamber and exhaust plus a door contact, LTE-M. Out-of-hours over-temperature fire alert, a cold-smoke temperature ceiling alarm, and a per-batch HACCP temperature record.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Failed underfloor heating beneath food-factory freezer stores lets frost heave crack the floor, causing six-figure repairs
problem: Freezer and blast-freezer stores sit on slabs with underfloor heating (glycol loops or electric mats) to stop the ground freezing. If the heating fails unnoticed for months, ice lenses lift the slab, racking goes out of plumb and the store must be emptied for repair (~£100k–£1m). Sub-floor temperatures are meant to be checked through probe tubes, but in SME factories nobody does it.
who_suffers: Factory owners, engineering teams and cold-store users
buyer: Engineering / Maintenance Manager of a food manufacturer with freezer stores
industry: Frozen-food manufacturers and processors with on-site freezer stores
current_workaround: Occasional manual readings of under-slab probes and refrigeration contractor checks. Nothing happens until the floor cracks.
sensor_concept: Thermistor strings dropped into the existing under-slab probe tubes, plus a current clamp on heater mats or the glycol pump. LoRaWAN. Alerts on a sub-zero subsoil trend or heater off, and a monthly record for insurers and the refrigeration contractor.
notes: c1: very high repair cost. c6: refrigeration contractors visit quarterly. c8: thermistor plus clamp. c2 (slow-developing, rare event) and c4 are weak.

title: Small food packers give away 2–4% extra product to stay legal on average weight, with paper ℮-mark records
problem: Packers using the ℮ mark must meet average-quantity rules and keep records of their checks under the Weights and Measures (Packaged Goods) Regulations 2006. Without checkweighers, small producers hand-weigh samples and deliberately overfill to be safe. A ~2% giveaway on £2m of output is ~£40k a year, and Trading Standards short-weight findings bring enforcement.
who_suffers: Owners and production staff
buyer: Owner / Operations Manager of an SME packer (bakery, confectionery, coffee, dried goods)
industry: SME food packers using manual or semi-automatic filling of ℮-marked prepacks
current_workaround: Bench scales, clipboard sample checks every 15–60 minutes and generous overfilling. Checkweighers (£10k+) are only on bigger lines.
sensor_concept: Retrofit load cell plus HX711 under an existing bench, or a cheap platform scale, with a LoRaWAN/cellular gateway (no factory Wi-Fi). Operators drop samples and the system logs weights, computes T1/T2 and average quantity per batch, alerts on drift and quantifies giveaway.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Food-factory effluent balancing tanks overflow when a pump trips at night, causing fish kills and EA prosecutions
problem: Dairies, meat plants and soft-drinks factories hold wash-water in balancing tanks or pump sumps before treatment or discharge to sewer. When a pump trips or level control sticks overnight, effluent overflows to surface-water drains and watercourses. Pollution prosecutions of food firms by the EA and water companies run from ~£10k to £1m+, and permits and consents require the system to be controlled.
who_suffers: Factory owners, environmental managers and the receiving river
buyer: Environmental / Engineering Manager of an SME food or soft-drinks manufacturer
industry: Dairies, meat processors, and soft-drink and juice producers with on-site effluent tanks
current_workaround: Local float alarms with a beacon and shift checks. Telemetry only on large sites.
sensor_concept: Float switches or a pressure level sensor in each sump or tank plus current clamps on transfer pumps, LTE-M. Out-of-hours alert on high level or pump fault, and a level and pump-run log as permit evidence.
notes: filtered: near-duplicate of R02-B-13 (effluent overflow fish kills)

title: Shellfish depuration tanks run with dead UV lamps or cold water, and norovirus outbreaks are traced back to the batch
problem: Live oysters, mussels and clams must be depurated in approved systems with working UV disinfection, adequate flow and a minimum water temperature for a minimum time, with batch records. A failed UV lamp or chiller makes depuration ineffective, and norovirus outbreaks lead to recalls, lost restaurant customers and harvesting restrictions (~£10k–£100k).
who_suffers: Shellfish producers, restaurants and consumers
buyer: Owner/Manager of a shellfish depuration centre or oyster farm
industry: Shellfish depuration and dispatch centres
current_workaround: Manual checks of the lamp-on indicator, thermometer and timer, written on batch sheets, with lamps replaced on the hour counter.
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the UV ballast, a temperature probe in the tank and a flow switch/pulse meter on recirculation, LTE-M. A button starts the batch timer. Alert on any fault mid-cycle, and an automatic batch record for food-authority inspections.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Small juice, dairy and soft-drink producers can't prove clean-in-place washes reached temperature and time
problem: Manual or semi-automatic CIP washes in small plants rely on operators, and a short or cool caustic cycle leaves biofilm. Product then spoils or is recalled (~£10k–£100k with retailer charge-backs). BRCGS/SALSA require cleaning to be validated and verified, and auditors ask for CIP records that small plants don't have.
who_suffers: Production teams and technical managers
buyer: Technical Manager / Owner of an SME juice, dairy or soft-drinks producer
industry: SME juice, smoothie, dairy and soft-drinks producers with manual CIP
current_workaround: Paper CIP sheets, operators reading dial thermometers, and ATP swabs after the clean.
sensor_concept: Clamp-on pipe temperature sensors on CIP return lines, a flow pulse meter and a current clamp on the CIP pump. LoRaWAN. Per-circuit record of time above set temperature, with alerts on short or cool washes.
notes: filtered: not in top ~50 at SORT

title: Hot-tub service firms make paid mid-stay visits to holiday-let tubs because they can't see whether each tub is heated, covered and circulating
problem: Independent hot-tub service companies look after dozens to hundreds of tubs at holiday cottages, lodges and glamping sites for absentee owners. Between changeovers they make scheduled or call-out visits because they can't see whether a tub has tripped, the cover was left off, the water level has dropped or the circulation pump has stopped (stagnant water is the HSG282 Legionella risk). A missed fault means a guest refund or an unsafe tub, and the owner is the one prosecuted (Piperdam lodge hot tub, £120k fine).
who_suffers: Service technicians driving to remote sites; absentee owners; guests
buyer: Owner / Operations Manager of a hot-tub servicing company selling holiday-let care plans (bills per changeover or per visit)
industry: Hot-tub maintenance contractors serving holiday cottages, lodges and glamping sites
current_workaround: Fixed changeover visits (parent evidence: ~£120+VAT per changeover package), mid-stay check visits, owners phoning guests, manual test strips logged on paper
sensor_concept: Per-tub LTE-M node with NO wetted chemistry probes: clamp-on pipe temperature on the heater return, CT clamp on the pump/heater supply (run hours, trips), reed switch on the cover (open-hours as a bather-load proxy), float switch for low water. Fleet dashboard ranks which tubs need a visit and auto-builds the HSG282 operational log (circulation, temperature, drain/refill events detected from level and temperature steps); technicians add strip readings in the app.
notes: Parent researcher proposed this buyer. Product cuts visits rather than replacing strip testing; need care-plan prices and number of UK hot-tub service firms.
fixes: c8: drops the parent's drifting ORP/pH probes for temperature, current, reed and float sensors (BOM plausibly <£50, no recalibration); c5: buyer is a service business that pays for every wasted truck roll and bills per visit, instead of a park ops manager with unevidenced budget; c7: a brand-agnostic multi-owner fleet view for contractors is not what pHin or OEM spa apps target; c6: the contractor is itself the channel.

title: Running display hot tubs in showrooms and at shows breed Legionella when circulation, disinfection and draining lapse between sales
problem: Hot-tub and swim-spa retailers, garden-centre concessions and exhibitors keep filled, heated display spas running for weeks to sell the 'wet demo'. Staff forget dosing and drain schedules. JTF Warehouse (Stoke, 2012: 21 cases, 2 deaths) was fined £1m because its display tub had not been cleaned for weeks with no disinfection programme; B&Q banned working displays after a Legionella finding; a US state-fair display spa outbreak killed 4. HSE's HSG282 covers display spas.
who_suffers: Showroom visitors and staff; the retailer facing prosecution
buyer: Owner / Managing Director of an independent hot-tub retailer (often multi-showroom); garden-centre group H&S manager
industry: Hot-tub and swim-spa showrooms, garden-centre spa concessions, home and garden shows
current_workaround: Paper HSG282 dosing and test-strip logs, weekly drain/refill by sales staff, or displaying tubs dry and losing the wet demo
sensor_concept: Per-display node: water temperature, CT clamp on the circulation pump (filtration hours), CT/pulse on the dosing pump or reed on the chemical feeder lid, level float plus temperature drop to detect drain-and-refill. Alerts when circulation stops, heating runs with no dosing activity, or water exceeds its drain interval. Exports an HSG282 display-spa log for EHOs.
notes: filtered: hot-tub family - kept M-01 and M-03
fixes: c1: niche-specific £1m fine plus outbreak deaths; c7: no product targets display-spa compliance; c8: no in-water chemistry probes; c5: owner-operator retailer holds the liability and buys directly; c6: spa manufacturers' dealer networks and trade bodies (BISHTA) reach every showroom.

title: Holiday-park operators carry the outbreak and reputation risk of privately owned, sublet lodge hot tubs they cannot see
problem: On many holiday parks, privately owned lodges and caravans with hot tubs are sublet by their owners to paying guests. The park operator has no visibility of whether owners' tubs are maintained to HSG282, yet the outbreak, guest complaints and press land on the park. Parks increasingly require owners to use the park's own hot-tub service.
who_suffers: Guests; the park's brand and licence; owners facing liability
buyer: Owner Services / Commercial Director of a multi-park holiday operator (sells service packages to lodge owners)
industry: Holiday parks with privately owned, sublet lodges and static caravans with hot tubs
current_workaround: Park rules requiring owners to buy the park's hot-tub service, staff spot checks, owners self-testing
sensor_concept: Same no-probe node as a contractor fleet (temperature, pump CT, cover reed, level float) plus a BLE tag proving technician visits. Park dashboard shows which owner tubs are circulating, heated and serviced; charged to owners monthly through the park's existing owner billing.
notes: Need evidence that parks mandate their own hot-tub services for sublet owner lodges (park owner rules / hot-tub policies).
fixes: c5/c9: the park monetises it as a recurring owner-services charge alongside pitch fees, so budget comes from an existing billing line; c6: the park is on site daily; c8: no probes; c7: nothing is sold to parks for oversight of owner tubs.

title: Holiday-let insurers cover guest illness and injury from hot tubs at thousands of cottages but have no evidence the tubs are run to HSG282
problem: Specialist holiday-let insurers and MGAs insure cottages and lodges whose hot tubs add guest illness and injury liability; they ask about hot tubs at quote but have no ongoing evidence the tub is maintained, so they load premiums or exclude hot tubs.
who_suffers: Insurer (public liability claims); owners facing exclusions; guests
buyer: Underwriting / Product Manager at a specialist holiday-let insurer or MGA
industry: Holiday-let and self-catering property insurance
current_workaround: Proposal-form questions, policy conditions requiring maintenance 'to HSG282', exclusions or premium loadings
